newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds fall further after Greenspan comments.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds fall further after Greenspan comments.

text.p: Irish bonds continued to fall in late trade on Wednesday, forced down by Tuesday's hawkish policy statement from the Irish Central Bank and later by comments from Fed chairman Alan Greenspan, dealers said.

In his semi-annual Humphrey Hawkins testimony to Congress, Greenspan said, among other things, that the Fed saw upside inflation risks and could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening of monetary policy.

"Irish prices were marked down early after yesterday's hawkish central bank policy statement. Trade this afternoon has been dominated by Greenspan's comments which were pretty negative. That has pushed us down further in line with overseas markets," Riada's Padraic Garvey said.
Garvey said Greenspan had succeeded in talking down both the U.S. equity and treasury markets in his speech.
"In his opinion, the Dow has gone ahead of itself. He would prefer to see it calm down and remain at the kind of levels it has fallen to today," Garvey said.
"In talking U.S. Treasury bonds down, he has forced yields up, forcing commercial and mortgage rates up as well. That seems to be what he wanted to do," he added.

The Dow industrials sold off sharply, losing 98 points or 1.4 percent, on Wednesday morning after Greenspan warned that the stock market's rise may be "unsustainable" while the Treasury market was also hit.

By 1614 GMT, the Irish 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 18 pence from Tuesday's close at 103.00 to yield 5.73 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 eased 30 pence from the close to 111.00 to yield 6.40 percent.
Dealers said Irish bonds were trading 133 basis points over German bunds in the five-year area and 85 basis points over Germany in the 10-year area.
